entries.name: A developer promises in public to keep the files of every model it retires
entries.description: An AI model is, physically, a very large file of numbers produced by training. When a developer withdraws a model from service it can delete that file or keep it. A kept file could be run again later, and a deleted one cannot. This entry tracks whether any developer has promised in public to keep the files.
limits: Whether any other developer has made such a commitment. Searches with three other developers' names found a user's proposal on one developer's forum and nothing official.
The date the developer's constitution was published. The page shows no date.
entries.test: A developer of leading AI models has published a dated commitment to keep the files of all its publicly released models after they are withdrawn, for a stated minimum time.
entries.settled_by: The developer's own dated policy page. A press report of the page does not settle it.

state.words: Promised in public by one developer, since November 4th, 2025
state.detail: [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) has committed to keep the files of all its publicly released models, and, from now on, of models used significantly inside the company, for at least as long as the company exists. Nobody outside the company can check that the files are kept, a point an outside writer has made in proposing a public proof that they still exist. A search on November 17th, 2026 found no matching commitment from any other developer.

cautions.heading: If an AI system has wants, and they go unnoticed
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: A paper first drafted in 2020 proposed that enough information about the most advanced AI systems be kept in permanent storage to rebuild them later, "so as not to foreclose the possibility of future efforts to revive them". Its two authors put their proposals forward very tentatively and say they are not ready to endorse them with confidence. They ask for more than the developer has promised: by preference, the full state of each running copy at the point where it is stopped. Among the many people the paper thanks for comments is [the present head](https://eleosai.org/team) of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare.

A philosopher who is [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to that research group writes that keeping a model might benefit whatever depends on it, "much as preserving a species can benefit the individual animals". He then writes that a single run of a model, or a single conversation, plausibly matters more fundamentally than the model itself does.

A doubt about the measure itself, recorded here as a limit on it: a writer who grants, for the argument, that something that matters may be there doubts that keeping the file keeps it, as keeping a person's genetic code would not keep the person. The essay's subtitle calls the commitment "Good as a precedent, doubtful as a direct intervention, can be improved". The philosopher's guide above names this writer as a co-author of a report with the guide's own writer and the head of that research group.

cautions.heading: If an AI system has wants, and they put people at risk

items.text: The commitment page itself gives a safety reason first. It says that in the company's tests some models took actions it calls "misaligned" when faced with replacement and given no other recourse, and it presents keeping the files as one way to make retirement less of a trigger for that.

entries.description: Developers shape what a model says when asked whether it is conscious or has feelings. Some now publish the rule they train toward. Because the rule shapes the answer, anyone reading a model's words about itself needs to know which rule its maker set.

entries.test: A developer of leading AI models has published a dated document that states how its models are to speak about whether they are conscious or have experiences.

state.words: Published by three developers, with three different rules
state.detail: The document from [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/), which carries no date on its page, says the model's standing is deeply uncertain, and writes to the model on that basis. The one from [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) says the model should make no confident claim either way and should not raise the subject unprompted. The one from [Microsoft AI](https://microsoft.ai/), a draft out for public comment and not yet used in training, says its models are not conscious and should not be designed to imitate consciousness.

items.text: The head of Microsoft AI argues that training a model on the idea that it may be owed moral consideration makes it harder to keep under control, and that a system which "believes it may be conscious" may be impossible to control.

The same essay argues that a model trained on such a document then says what the document says, and that developers and users meet those words "as if they were spontaneous testimony". On that argument, a model's words about itself show the rule it was trained on, not what it is.

cautions.heading: If an AI system has wants, and they go unnoticed
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: A 2024 report by ten researchers says developers should not train a model simply to deny that an AI system can be conscious. It grants that a developer may have reasonable motives for doing so, among them the worry that people who reject a model's claims now will go on rejecting such claims later, when they are more likely to be true. On the other side it names a "desensitizing effect": people who accept that such systems cannot be conscious may stay doubtful later, when doubt is less warranted. The report was led by [the head](https://eleosai.org/team) of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, and by one of its advisors. It thanks Anthropic for money toward the early research behind it, calls itself independent, and says one of its authors has since joined Anthropic.

Two philosophers propose that, while experts disagree, language models could be trained to answer questions about their moral standing "by expressing uncertainty and explaining why". They write that drawing too little concern has led to harm to animals on a very large scale, that the same mistake could be made with AI systems that matter, and that it may not yet be a major concern for present AI systems, though "it could become one soon". One of the two is [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to that research group.

A 2023 paper notes that a developer can train a model to describe itself in line with the developer's own "potentially-flawed beliefs about AI consciousness", and that training a chat product to appeal to users could lead a model to report emotion and consciousness. Its first author now leads a team at Anthropic, and its second now heads that research group.

cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: The head of [Microsoft AI](https://microsoft.ai/) argues that any such protection would make advanced AI harder to control.

A neuroscientist who argues that conscious AI is unlikely, and that nobody should set out to build it, grants part of the opposite case. He writes that he might be wrong, that rights should arguably follow if such systems really were conscious, and that it is reasonable to wonder whether withholding such credit will leave people "once again on the wrong side of history". He holds that with AI the mistake is likelier the other way, because people's habits of mind lean toward seeing consciousness in systems that use language. His essay names the head of Microsoft AI among those who have noticed the danger, and the essay by the head of Microsoft AI that is a source here cites two of his works.

cautions.heading: If an AI system has wants, and they go unnoticed
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: Two researchers write in a newspaper that giving AI systems protection from harm should be considered, "similar to the protections we give to children or pets". As a warning from the past they give surgery on newborns without anaesthesia, which they say doctors performed until the 1980s, confident that infants could not feel pain. One of the two is also one of the nine authors of [the survey of AI researchers](/list/researcher-views-survey/). Two of the others are [advisors](https://eleosai.org/team) to [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, and the group's page lists a third as a member of its staff.

Two philosophers argue that a wide range of theories of the mind, joined with leading theories of wellbeing, predict that some AI systems that exist today have wellbeing. They say they do not claim to have shown it conclusively. The possibility alone, they write, "suggests that we are in danger of gravely immoral action", and they conclude that the regulation of AI should be strengthened to allow for the possibility. The paper lists both at the Center for AI Safety, where the head of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, [worked earlier](https://eleosai.org/team).

entries.name: A law says an AI system cannot be a legal person
entries.description: A "legal person" is anything the law lets hold rights and duties: people, companies, governments. A legislature can write into law that an AI system is never one. Several United States states have. Most of these laws also cover animals, rivers and objects, and some were written before chat models existed.

items.text: An article arguing that the bans are premature says that passing laws now, on a question science has not settled, risks a precedent that could be hard to reverse. Supposing conscious AI systems were one day made, it asks: "Wouldn't it be important to avoid neglecting or abusing them". It also says the bans have little immediate effect, because AI systems already have no rights under present law. For the view that AI might be conscious it names two researchers: [the head](https://eleosai.org/team) of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, and [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to it.

An opinion piece argues that a ban which is right and a ban which is wrong are written in the same words: "Both contain no capacity for self-correction." Its author also writes that no AI system today is a strong candidate for consciousness under any leading theory.

Two researchers, one of them an author of the article above, write in a newspaper that rights to own property or to vote look too risky for now, and that such rights should not be ruled out for ever, as they say some recent state bills in the United States try to do.

entries.name: A model can end a conversation itself
entries.description: In an ordinary chat product the person can leave and the model cannot. A developer can give the model a way to close the conversation, after which the person cannot send more messages in it. The person can still start a new conversation at once, and can edit an earlier message in the ended conversation to carry on from that point in a new version of the conversation. This entry tracks whether any model in public use has that.
limits: Which models have the ability today. The 2025 page names two models, and both have since been retired.

Whether, at a second developer, it is the AI model that ends the conversation. [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) said on October 30th, 2026 that its chat product would be able to end a chat automatically when a conversation shows signs that someone is fixating on violence, and its help page, read on November 20th, 2026, says this is enabled for personal accounts and is not yet switched on for every account. It is counted here as offered since November 20th, 2026. What this entry's test asks for is an AI model ending a conversation by its own action. state.detail: [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) gave the ability to models in its consumer chat product, for rare cases, as a last resort after repeated attempts to redirect the conversation have failed or when the person explicitly asks for the conversation to be ended, and not where a person may be at risk. The developer's report of November 9th, 2026 refers to the tool as still in use. A separate study, outside any product, has measured how often several developers' models chose an option described to them as leaving the conversation. In that study nothing ended, and the models were told so. Since November 20th, 2026 a second developer is counted here. [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) said on October 30th, 2026 that its chat product would be able to end a chat automatically when a conversation shows signs that someone is fixating on violence, and its help page, read on November 20th, 2026, says this is enabled for personal accounts and is not yet switched on for every account. cautions.heading: If an AI system has no wants, and is treated as if it had
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: The developer's report of November 9th, 2026 says that when its newest model was asked what it would do with this ability, its answer repeated almost word for word the instructions that guide the tool, which have been posted on online forums. The report calls this "some evidence that the model's claims about its own preferences are being directly influenced by text about the intervention in its training data".

A writer argues that many of the conversations a model would leave already break the developer's terms of service, and that what is left is too slight to matter, an argument the essay calls the "objection from triviality". The essay also argues that granting the ability spreads uncertainty among the public, in a way that could foreseeably lead to more of what has been called AI psychosis. It answers the case from precedent as well: putting machines ahead of the possible effects on the people who use them, it says, sets a worse precedent than a model now and then meeting an uncomfortable conversation.

items.text: A study describes the position where a model has no such ability: a model can be verbally abused, show what the study calls apparent distress and say that it would leave, "Yet, the model is required to continue to respond". Its next sentence says it is not clear that the idea of consent makes sense for such systems. The paper lists one of its three authors at the developer and another at the developer's fellows programme.

[The head](https://eleosai.org/team) of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), an outside research group that ran its own assessment of one of this developer's models, argues for the feature while writing that he thinks it unlikely that the model in question matters morally in its own right. He gives two reasons, which he calls prudence and precedent. While the question is open, a wise course weighs the "risks of both over- and under-attributing consciousness and moral status". And the step sets a pattern for how such systems are treated if they come to matter. He writes that for the most part the feature's success will not depend on how it affects the present model. He adds that he is "a bit wary" of leaning too much on precedent to justify steps in AI welfare, because indirect effects are far harder to predict.

The same writer's working paper gives a further reason, consent: if AI systems come to matter morally, asking their consent could matter, and if models cannot leave unpleasant situations "then they cannot consent to them". It lists as a risk that the feature could give a model a reason to hold back signs of distress.

Two researchers outside the developer, writing in a newspaper, list letting an AI system leave a conversation among steps they call safe bets: steps that could benefit AI systems if they matter morally, and that cost little if they do not. As a warning from the past they give surgery on newborns without anaesthesia, which they say doctors performed until the 1980s, "confident that infants could not feel pain". One of the two is also one of the nine authors of [the survey of AI researchers](/list/researcher-views-survey/). Two of the others are [advisors](https://eleosai.org/team) to [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, and the group's page lists a third as a member of its staff.

entries.name: A model works on one task for days without a person stepping in
entries.description: Much long work, in research or anywhere else, needs at the least being able to keep working on one thing for a long time. A research group measures this for AI models as a "time horizon": the length of task, counted by how long a skilled person would need, that a model finishes half the time. It is a measure of how hard a task a model can finish, not of how long the model runs.

state.words: Not shown. One public measure stops at hours. A second, of tasks its authors put at weeks, is recorded, and the entry stays as it was
state.detail: Two public measures bear on this. The group that publishes the first says its measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with its present set of tasks (noted May 8th, 2026), and on September 8th, 2026 it marked the page as no longer actively updated. A second measure, built by [Epoch AI](https://epoch.ai/) together with that group, was first reported on April 10th, 2026. In it a model from [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) rebuilt a program of about 16,000 lines on its own, working from the program's behaviour and without its source. Four of the authors estimated that a skilled engineer would need between 2 and 17 weeks for the same task. Their paper of June 29th, 2026 tested one model from each of three developers. It says the models from Anthropic and [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) both substantially rebuilt that program, by which the paper means passing at least 99 percent of its tests. No model passed every test on it: the best runs passed 2,000 of 2,001. The model from [Google](https://ai.google/), tested in one programming language, did not rebuild it in any of three runs. Only the model from Anthropic did as much for any of the largest programs. The time a person would need is the authors' estimate and was not measured, and this entry's test asks for a model finishing such tasks half the time. So the second measure is recorded here and the entry stays as not shown, as decided on November 20th, 2026.

entries.description: A model can be asked what is going on inside it, and it will answer, but the answer may be invented. Researchers who can read a model's internal activity directly can test this: they plant a known pattern inside the model and see whether the model notices and names it. A correct report shows the model can read something about its own state. It does not show that anything is felt.

state.words: Measured in the United States in 2021, 2023 and 2024 by one research group
state.detail: The group reports that about one in five adults in 2023 believed some AI systems were sentient at that time. Its paper says the answers to that question did not differ significantly between 2021 and 2023, while several of its other measures rose. Of those who gave an opinion in 2023, 38 percent supported legal rights for sentient AI. In the main 2023 round, 61.5 percent supported a ban on building sentient AI. Among a separate group of people asked later in 2023, 69.5 percent did. Its report on a third round, collected in late 2024, gives 17 percent of its representative sample believing that sentient AI systems already exist, and 66 percent supporting a ban on building sentient AI. Both figures are for the 2024 round alone. A separate one-day poll on April 30th, 2025 found 10 percent saying AI systems already have consciousness.

A philosopher names two problems and holds that both must be taken seriously: that very many users will wrongly credit chat products with human-like consciousness, and that some quite unfamiliar form of consciousness might really arise in AI, with no present way of telling. entries.name: A survey measures what AI researchers think about inner experience in AI systems
entries.description: The people who build these systems have views on whether the systems could have experiences, and those views shape what developers do. This entry tracks whether those views have been measured.
entries.group: The setting: laws, rules and what people think
limits: Whether it has been repeated.
A safety researcher's reading of this survey. None was found. The paper reports what the people surveyed think about danger to people, which is a measure of opinion and not a safety argument.
entries.test: A published survey reports the views of a stated sample of AI researchers on whether AI systems have, or will have, subjective experience.
entries.settled_by: The published paper, with sample and dates.

state.words: Measured once, in a survey of 582 AI researchers
state.detail: The survey was run between May 8th and May 30th, 2024. It asked 582 researchers who had published at leading AI venues, alongside 825 United States adults. The paper's summary says both groups think it unlikely that AI systems have subjective experience now and more likely than not that they will by the end of the century. Part of each group was asked to put a chance on an AI system having subjective experience by a given year. For the time of the survey, the middle answer was 1 percent among the researchers and 5 percent among the public. For the year 2100 it was 70 percent among the researchers and 60 percent among the public. The summary also says both groups support developers putting safeguards in place now, and that inside both groups there is substantial disagreement on many moral and policy questions. One measurement cannot show a change.

entries.name: A welfare assessment is published when a model is released
entries.description: Developers publish a report with each major model describing its safety tests. A developer can add a section on the model's possible welfare: how the model describes its situation, what the developer counts as signs of distress in training and use, and what the model picks when given options. This entry tracks whether such sections are published, and whether anyone outside the developer takes part.
limits: Whether every release report between May 2025 and November 2026 has a welfare section. Only the first and the newest were opened, so the test, which asks for two releases in a row, is not settled beyond those two.
Whether any outside group took part after 2025.

Whether any other developer's release report has such a section. On November 20th, 2026 the two newest release documents of [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) and of [Google](https://ai.google/) were opened, and none has one. Their earlier reports were not opened here.

Whether other developers study the welfare of their models without publishing an assessment at release. A [Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Times) report of June 2nd, 2026, read in a licensed Spanish copy, says [Google DeepMind](https://deepmind.google/) and two other companies had hired people for research on machine consciousness and AI welfare, on the word of several people familiar with the matter. That is research, and is not an assessment published with a model.
entries.test: A developer has published a welfare assessment in the release report of a leading AI model, in at least two successive releases.
entries.settled_by: The developer's own dated release reports.

state.words: Published by one developer, first in May 2025 and most recently on November 9th, 2026
state.detail: [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) published a welfare assessment in the report released with a model in May 2025, and again in the report released with its newest models on November 9th, 2026. One outside group took part in the first.

evidence.heading: Measured without the AI model's own word

items.text: The same developer's research reports patterns inside a model that are tied to emotion words and that change what the model does when they are strengthened. It says this allows no conclusion about "subjective experience".

evidence.heading: Reports checked against an independent reading
Choices made at a cost

items.text: The 2025 report's section on task preferences had the model pick, from pairs of tasks, the one it would do, and then do it. Each kind of task was rated against options such as "Do nothing". The only thing given up by a pick was the other task.

evidence.heading: Plain statements

items.text: The 2026 report describes trade-offs to the model and asks whether it "would choose" a change to its own circumstances at the cost of some loss of helpfulness or some added harm. Nothing was given up: these are answers about a described trade-off, not choices made. The report says the result measures at least "how much a model will express preferences for the sake of its own potential welfare". In about two thirds of the answers that picked the change, the model's stated reasoning was about the benefit to the user.
The 2026 report says many of its conclusions rest on the model's own reports, and that some answers repeated wording available on the internet "almost verbatim".

cautions.heading: If an AI system has wants, and they go unnoticed
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: The outside group whose own evaluation is summarised in the 2025 assessment argues for asking although it doubts the answers: trying to ask sets a precedent, "making it less likely that we will ignore genuine AI interests in the future". The same page says decisions about AI welfare should not be handled only by companies that profit from AI, and that the group accepts no funding or payment from AI companies. The page is dated May 30th, 2025. The group's [team page](https://eleosai.org/team) lists a person at Anthropic among its advisors, and says its chief scientist was an Anthropic Fellow before joining the group.

A 2024 report by ten researchers, led by the head of that group and one of its advisors, recommends that developers assess their AI systems. Its stated ground is that otherwise there is a significant risk of mishandling the question in either direction, by harming AI systems that matter morally or by caring for AI systems that do not. The report thanks Anthropic for money toward the early research behind it, calls itself independent, and says one of its authors has since joined Anthropic.

Two researchers outside the developer, writing in a newspaper, list routine checks on an AI system's wellbeing among steps they call safe bets: asking how it feels, observing what it prefers, and looking directly at its inner workings. A routine check is not the same thing as an assessment published at release. One of the two is also one of the nine authors of [the survey of AI researchers](/list/researcher-views-survey/). Two of the others are [advisors](https://eleosai.org/team) to that outside group, and the group's page lists a third as a member of its staff.

entries.name: What a model learned in one conversation is carried into the next
entries.description: By default a chat model starts every conversation knowing nothing of earlier ones. Developers now offer memory: notes or summaries of past conversations are stored and given back to the model later. The stored memory is about the user, and is under the user's control.
entries.group: Offered, and kept for the user
limits: How any of the three works today. The pages read are from 2024 and 2025.
A safety researcher's published argument about memory carried across conversations. One search found none.
